launches.body:
We're building Zomma: AI operations employees for finance back offices, starting with cross-border transaction alert investigations.

**TL;DR:** Zomma agents work directly inside the software your ops team already uses. No APIs, no integrations. For every cross-border alert, the agent gathers the evidence, writes the draft assessment, and drafts the RFI, end-to-end. Running live compliance-ops pilots with a US RIA and a $10B AUM wealth tech. 92% on OSWorld.

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oDXDKH_tYhg>

## **The problem**

Cross-border payments trip more monitoring rules than anything else in the queue: sanctions name hits on foreign counterparties, high-risk corridors, first-time beneficiaries. Most alerts are false positives (McKinsey: over 90% in transaction monitoring), but every one still needs to be investigated. 20 to 60 minutes per case, across five or six systems, several with no API at all. And the evidence that clears them sits in foreign company registries and local-language adverse media. 

So review capacity scales the only way it can: hiring. When hiring lags volume, alerts pile into backlogs that take months to clear, and backlogs are what regulators fine: $3.8B in AML penalties last year alone.

## **What Zomma does**

Zomma agents work the queue on the same screens your analysts use: case manager, screening tool, admin panel, inbox, web search. Onboarding looks like hiring: an SOP and a login.

On a transaction monitoring alert, the agent

* pulls the KYC profile and payment history
* verifies the invoice and researches the counterparty, including registries you can only search by hand
* writes a case-specific assessment with every claim cited to the source screen
* drafts the RFI when documents are missing

Every step is logged and replayable: timestamped screenshots of every page checked, numbered citations, explicit no-match statements, a screen-by-screen trail an examiner can follow.

## **Why start with cross-border alerts**

If an employee can do it on a screen, Zomma can learn it: the rest of the compliance queue, payment disputes, client onboarding, trade ops. Cross-border alerts come first because they have the exact shape our agents are best at: high-volume, parallelizable work that needs real reasoning but follows a defined workflow to a documented disposition. They're also the hardest cases to automate any other way: the evidence lives in registries and portals that will never have APIs. And agents scale with the queue: a volume spike means provisioning two more that afternoon; a BPO batch takes a month to train.

launches.body:
**Hey YC!**

We're Rohan, Dev, and Tommy, and we're building Praxis.

**Praxis turns real-world work into training data for robots.**

<https://youtu.be/xri7vyzxW-I?si=L6ZBgLO24OrvYuuH>

**What we do**

Robots learn to act in the physical world by watching humans do the work. We partner with businesses to capture egocentric human demonstration data, the first-person video of how tasks actually get done in factories, warehouses, homes, and other physical work environments, then supply it to the labs and humanoid teams training the next generation of robots. Robotics data is our focus, but since our collection infrastructure overlaps, we're happy to explore other multimodal data too.

**The problem**

Robotics is missing its internet-scale training corpus. LLMs learned from the web, books, code, and the accumulated record of human thought. Robots need the equivalent record of human action: how people pick, pack, clean, assemble, inspect, cook, use tools, recover from mistakes, and move through messy physical environments.

Collecting some of this data is easy. Collecting enough of the right kind is brutally hard, for two reasons.

First, diversity is capped by access. Models only generalise if they've seen the full range of real environments and operators, from a one-person shop to a national-scale industrial operation. Getting in the door across that entire spectrum, and across continents, is a physical-world access problem that most teams can't solve.

Second, it takes two rare skills at once. You have to know what frontier labs need at a technical level, and be able to run demanding physical operations across thousands of real sites, standardising capture and turning fragmented workflows into model-ready data. Few teams have both halves.

**Our solution**

We already run collections across 150 environment types on 5 continents, with diversity from mom-and-pop stores to conglomerates accounting for 3% of a nation's GDP, and a reachable network of 60,000 workers. Depending on the task, we capture egocentric video, stereo-RGB, IMU, wrist-camera views, glove kinematics, haptics, and dense annotations. Everything is delivered calibrated, synced, pose-tracked, QA'd, and PII-scrubbed. We build and deploy custom capture hardware quickly because part of the team operates out of Shenzhen.

**Why us**

Praxis is built to do both hard things at once. We pair robotics research depth (IEEE, NASA JPL) with the ability to actually run demanding operations in the real world, from Fortune 500 supply chains to Parliaments, plus a Shenzhen hardware team. That combination- technical understanding of what labs need plus real physical-world access at scale- is what lets us deliver diverse, model-ready data at a cost and breadth that is irreplaceable.

**Our asks**

1. Intros to anyone working on robotics, embodied AI, or world-models, especially data and research leads. If you need other forms of multimodal data, we're happy to explore that too.
2. If you run a business with interesting physical work (logistics, manufacturing, food, retail, or lab work) and would like to monetize it, we'd love to talk.

You can reach us at [founders@praxisrobotics.io](mailto:founders@praxisrobotics.io) and [rohan@praxisrobotics.io](mailto:rohan@praxisrobotics.io)[ https://www.praxisrobotics.io](https://www.praxisrobotics.io)

launches.body:
Hi everyone - Stan and Jonas here, founders of **Grip**. We build intelligent robots that sort _any_ waste, not just the clean, predictable objects existing systems are limited to. We're starting with plastic contamination in organic waste.\
\
<https://youtu.be/qIJ4a49WxpI>

**The problem**

We didn't start with a thesis, we found it on sorting lines, after visiting waste facilities across several countries:

* **Contamination is existential.** Plastic that organic-waste facilities can't remove gets shredded, processed, and spread onto agricultural soil. Operators spend up to 30% of operating costs fighting it and still fall short. Even Germany's 0.1% limit for plastic in finished compost is a tacit admission that full removal isn't possible with today's tools.
* **The labor force is aging and shrinking.** The picking work is unpleasant and turnover is brutal. Operators increasingly aren't choosing between people and robots. They're choosing between robots and nobody.
* **Dangerous items cause fires.** Batteries, propane tanks, and vapes slip through and ignite during handling and shredding: 448 reported fires at US and Canadian waste facilities in 2025, \~$2.5B in damage, and insurers are walking away. At the same time trash sorting is sitting in the top 5 of US deadliest occupations.

**What we built**

The hard part isn't the gripper. It's that waste never looks the way you planned. Objects arrive crushed, folded, tangled, half-buried, and moving. Put today's sorting robots in front of this and they break.

We're building one manipulation system that picks whatever shows up, at the front of the line where the material is most chaotic and existing automation stops. That means chaotic scene understanding, robust grasp planning, and hardware built for real waste streams: our custom three-way gripper is designed to maximize throughput, taking out as much contamination per cycle as possible.

Our rugged hardware matters, but intelligence is the product. Every pick generates data no other system ever encounters: what the robot saw, what it tried, how the material responded, whether it worked.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=111317&key=user_uploads/3678142/bc867fdc-9225-4b85-83f9-f83433465d5b)

**Why now**

Waste policy has moved from vague ambition to enforceable deadlines:

* Separate bio-waste collection is now mandatory across the EU. More material, and more contamination, every year.
* New EU fertiliser rules just cut permitted impurities in compost and digestate, with national limits like Germany's stricter still.
* The US is real: California mandated a 75% cut in landfilled organics, missed it, and enforcement is ramping. At the same time, landfills near major cities are filling up, and that pressure is pushing more and more US municipalities to collect organic waste separately. More material, more contamination, more facilities that need to sort it.

More than 6,500 biowaste plants and thousands of recycling facilities across Europe and North America face this with no robot that can touch it. That's Grip.

**Why us**

We've built autonomous race cars, quadrupeds, drones, and excavators, robots that operate in dirt, weather, and chaos rather than controlled labs. Grip is that experience applied to an industry where physical intelligence removes a real bottleneck.

**Our ask**

We'd love intros to:

* Owners and operators of composting, anaerobic-digestion, and organic-waste facilities
* Owners and operators of MRFs and recycling facilities
* Regulators and experts shaping contamination limits and recycling standards

If someone runs a facility and will show us their hardest sorting problem, we'll get on a plane.
